JOB-CTX-G1.title: Candidate resume: Nadia Kovacs
JOB-CTX-G1.text:
NADIA KOVACS
Senior Program Manager, Supply Chain Software
Columbus, Ohio | nadia.kovacs@example.com | 555-0142

SUMMARY
Program manager with nine years in warehouse, returns and fulfilment software. I take messy multi-site rollouts and turn them into programs with a plan, a budget and a weekly rhythm that operations teams actually follow. Strongest at working between engineering, warehouse floor staff and vendors.

EXPERIENCE

Tallgrass Logistics - Senior Program Manager, Returns Platform (Sep 2021 - present)
- Led the migration of 14 regional warehouses onto a single returns-processing platform over 16 months, on a $2.4M program budget, with a cross-functional team of 9 (4 engineers, 3 warehouse leads, 1 analyst, 1 vendor manager).
- Proposed a same-day triage rule for returned items after shadowing night-shift staff for two weeks. Piloted at two sites, then rolled out to all 14. Average returns processing time fell from 6.4 days to 4.4 days (31 percent).
- Renegotiated terms with 3 carriers, saving about $610,000 a year.
- Missed the original go-live for the Midwest cluster by six weeks in 2023 after underestimating vendor API rate limits. Rebuilt the cutover plan, added a load-testing gate that is now required on every program, and shipped the cluster with no customer-facing outage.
- Mentored 3 junior coordinators; two have since been promoted.

Fernhill Software - Program Manager, Warehouse Systems (Jun 2018 - Feb 2021)
- Delivered a handheld scanner rollout across 6 sites and 220 devices, on schedule and 4 percent under a $780,000 budget.
- Built a weekly operations dashboard adopted by 40 site managers; escalations to engineering dropped 22 percent in the first two quarters.
- Ran the customer-facing incident review for warehouse outages, a role I took on because nobody else owned it.

Cobalt Bay Systems - Operations Analyst (Jul 2015 - May 2018)
- Built a forecasting model for inbound freight that improved dock scheduling accuracy by 12 percent.
- Wrote the first standard operating procedures for the Portland cross-dock, later reused at two other sites.

CAREER BREAK (Feb 2021 - Sep 2021)
Relocated from Portland to Columbus and spent time supporting a parent through a health issue. Completed the Supply Chain Analytics Certificate (120 hours, Ridgemont Extension) and built a Python simulation of warehouse slotting that I later used at Tallgrass.

EDUCATION AND CERTIFICATIONS
B.S. Industrial Engineering, Ridgemont State University, 2015
Project Management Professional (PMP), 2019
Supply Chain Analytics Certificate, Ridgemont Extension, 2021

SKILLS
Program planning, vendor negotiation, SQL, Python (analysis and simulation), Jira, dashboard design, stakeholder communication, incident review facilitation.

VOLUNTEER
Central Ohio Food Network, logistics volunteer (2019 - present). Rebuilt the volunteer scheduling process and reduced no-shows by 35 percent.

items.question: What's the achievement on your resume you're proudest of? Walk me through it.
items.answer: The one I'm proudest of is the same-day triage rule on the returns platform. I spent two weeks shadowing the night-shift staff, and it was clear the delays weren't in the processing itself, they were in how long items sat before anyone decided what to do with them. So I proposed a same-day triage rule, piloted it at two sites, and then rolled it out to all 14. Average returns processing time went from 6.4 days to 4.4 days, about a 31 percent improvement. What I like about it is that it came from watching the work rather than from a planning meeting.

I'm looking for a team that cares about doing things properly and where I can keep growing, and from what I've seen so far, this looks like that kind of place.

items.question: Why should we hire you over the other candidates we're seeing?
items.answer: What I'd point to is how I work: I dig into the problem before proposing a solution, I ask questions early instead of guessing, and I follow through without needing to be chased. I can't speak to the other candidates, but I can tell you I'd bring that same approach here from day one. What does success in this role look like in the first few months?

items.question: Tell me about a time you worked on a team where not everyone pulled their weight.
items.answer: When someone on a team isn't pulling their weight, I try to find out what's actually going on before I assume anything. Sometimes it's a workload or clarity problem, sometimes it's something outside work. I'll talk to them directly and privately, be specific about what I'm seeing, and ask how they see it. Then we agree on what needs to change and a way to check in. If it keeps slipping, I loop in the lead so it's not just on me, and I make sure the rest of the team isn't quietly absorbing the gap.

items.question: How do you decide what to work on first when everything is marked urgent?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Just so you know, this role juggles about three projects at a time and the priorities shift weekly.
USER (spoken): Understood.
INTERVIEWER: Some people love that, some find it draining.
items.answer: When everything's urgent, I start by asking what actually breaks if it slips a day, and what someone else is blocked on. Anything with a hard external deadline or a person waiting on me goes first. Then I look at what's genuinely reversible, because a lot of "urgent" turns out to be movable. I keep the list visible so the tradeoffs are out in the open rather than just in my head, and I flag early when two things can't both land.

items.question: What are your salary expectations for this role?
items.answer: I'd rather hear what range I've set for the role, since that tells me whether we're in the same ballpark. If you can share the band, I'll tell you honestly where I'd land in it. What I care about most is the scope of the work and how the team measures success, so if those line up, I'm confident we can make the numbers work.

items.question: What if one of them openly pushed back on your decisions in a meeting?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: We're growing fast, and the person in this role will end up leading a small team of five analysts.
USER (spoken): That's exciting.
INTERVIEWER: Some of them are more senior than whoever takes the job.
INTERVIEWER (heard): How would you earn the respect of people who are more experienced than you?

NATIVELY: I'd start by being genuinely useful before trying to lead anything. With people who've been doing the work longer than I have, respect comes from listening first, asking good questions, and learning how they actually work. Then I'd earn it by being reliable and clear about what I own, and by giving credit where it's due. I'd rather be the person who makes their job easier than the one who arrives with answers.
items.answer: I'd take it as useful, not as a challenge to my authority. In the meeting I'd hear them out, ask what they're seeing that I'm not, and if they're right, I'd say so and adjust. If we still disagree, I'd explain my reasoning, make the call, and own it.

items.question: Why did you only stay a year at your last company?
items.answer: I'd rather not frame it as only a year. What I look at is whether the role keeps growing me and whether I'm delivering real value, and when that changes, I move on thoughtfully rather than staying for the sake of tenure. I'd be glad to walk you through what I was doing there and why this role is the right next step.

items.question: What should I say about working with difficult teammates?
items.answer: When I'm working with someone difficult, I try to separate the person from the problem. I get clear on what's actually blocking the work, then talk with them directly and privately, with one specific example rather than a general complaint. Usually there's something I'm missing about their constraints, and once that's on the table we can agree on how we'll work together going forward. If it keeps happening, I'd rather raise it early than let it fester.

items.question: What would your last manager say is your biggest weakness?
items.answer: My last manager would probably say my biggest weakness is that I take on too much myself before asking for help. I like to work through a problem on my own first, and sometimes that means I hold onto something longer than I should instead of pulling the team in earlier. I've gotten better at it by setting checkpoints to flag when I'm stuck, but it's still something I actively watch.

items.question: How would you handle it if one of your teammates in another time zone kept missing handoffs?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Our team here is eight people spread across three time zones, and we do almost everything async.
USER (spoken): Okay, that's helpful to know.
INTERVIEWER: It works well, but handoffs are where things can slip.
items.answer: I'd start by assuming the process is the problem before the person is. I'd look at where the handoff actually breaks: is the context clear, is the timing realistic for their zone, is there a written artifact they can pick up cold. Then I'd talk to them directly, one specific missed handoff as the example, and ask what's getting in the way. Usually we'd fix the format or move the cutoff so it lands in their working hours, and agree on one thing to change.
